partial.pre: This prescription governs, Apprendi determined, even if the State characterizes the additional findings made by the judge as “sentencing factor[s].” Id., at 492.
partial.quote: Apprendi's reasoning is irreconcilable with Walton’s holding in this regard, and today we overrule Walton in relevant part.
partial.post: Capital defendants, no less than noncapital defendants, we conclude, are entitled to a jury determination of any fact on which the legislature conditions an increase in their maximum punishment.
holdings: A state capital sentencing scheme does not violate the Sixth Amendment merely because aggravating circumstances are found by the judge rather than a jury.
Arizona’s allocation of the burden of proof in capital sentencing does not violate the Constitution.
A capital sentencing statute is not unconstitutionally mandatory if it does not automatically impose death upon conviction for specified murders.
An aggravating circumstance defined by a state supreme court is constitutionally sufficient if, despite lack of mathematical precision, it gives the sentencer meaningful guidance.
When a capital sentencing factor has been given a constitutionally sufficient narrowing construction, proportionality review is not constitutionally required.

led.name: Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.
led.holding: An employment practice committed without improper purpose or discriminatory intent is not unlawful merely because it gives effect to an intentional discriminatory act that occurred outside the charge-filing period.

split.question: Does the phrase 'prison conditions' in 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a) encompass particular incidents of prison life, including isolated assaults or excessive force?

sides.name: Booth v. Churner
sides.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
sides.quote: We reject this argument and hold that § 1997e(a) applies to excessive force actions.

sides.name: Nussle v. Willette
sides.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
sides.quote: Because we conclude that § 1997e(a) does not apply to allegations of particular instances of excessive force or assault by prison employees, we vacate the District Court’s judgment and remand for reinstatement of Nussle’s complaint.

sides.name: Porter v. Nussle
sides.court: Supreme Court of the United States
sides.quote: We reject both readings and hold, in line with the text and purpose of the PLRA, our precedent in point, and the weight of lower court authority, that §1997e(a)’s exhaustion requirement applies to all prisoners seeking redress for prison circumstances or occurrences.
